sentences.t: IRDAI member Girija Subramanian said the distribution reforms could start on 1 January or 1 April 2027, with commission caps ahead of the phased expense cuts, because phasing commissions would invite a rush of sales before each cut (Insurer Flux, Medianama, Insurance Reporter).
The Sensex rose 1,109.10 points, 1.54%, to 73,033.78, its best day in four months.
The Nifty gained 358.60 to 22,721.95.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the debate on long-term capital gains tax and securities transaction tax is healthy, and the buying picked up (BusinessLine, CNBC-TV18, ET Now).
Nifty IT gained 5.22%.
HCLTech's results and a global scare over AI financing lifted the sector, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying capital is the next limit on the AI build-out (ET, Finology).
Korea's KOSPI fell about 5.5% as Samsung and SK Hynix dropped 7% to 10% on reports that China's CXMT is moving up in memory chips (ET Now, Yahoo Finance, Hindustan Times).
Foreign banks are circling Indian lenders: MUFG is weighing majority control of Shriram Finance, and Abu Dhabi's IHC is in early talks on a stake in Bandhan Bank's promoter.
Both stocks jumped 6% to 9%, both on press reports (Moneycontrol, Mint, Business Today).
Google released Gemini 4 Argon on 13 October with a one-million-token context window.
Its introductory API price is $2 per million input tokens until 30 November (Google).
Sarvam AI is reported to be in talks to raise up to $300 million at about a $3 billion valuation, roughly double its current one.
F2A, a Nandan Nilekani-anchored fund, has ₹3,000 crore in subscriptions (ET, BusinessLine).
One Concept a Day: the first-offer anchor, from a 2001 negotiation paper by Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler.
It is directly useful for commission and salary talks.

IRDAI (India's insurance regulator) whole-time member for distribution Girija Subramanian said in an interview with Bloomberg, as relayed by Insurer Flux and Medianama, that the regulator is considering 1 January or 1 April 2027 as start dates for its reform paper Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution.
Commission caps would start before the phased cuts to expense limits.
The reason she gave: phasing in commission cuts could push distributors to rush sales ahead of each reduction, which raises the risk of mis-selling.
So the fast track on commissions is a conduct argument, not only a cost argument.
Expense limits are different.
They phase over five years, with the first interim step in the year ending March 2029, per Insurer Flux.
Draft rules follow the 25 October comment deadline, then another round of public comment before the final rules.
The case the regulator is making, from IRDAI's own data as reported by The Insurance Reporter: between FY23 and FY25, life corporate-agent premium grew 28% while payouts to them grew 125%.
Broker premium in general insurance grew 37% while commissions grew 173%.
In motor, premium grew about 34% and commissions about 259%.
Private life insurers now spend about 22% of premium on expenses, up from 16% in FY21.
Private general insurers spend about 32%, up from 25% in FY19.
The pushback has numbers too.

The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI, the brokers' trade body) says broker revenue could fall 60% to 70% and up to one million jobs are at risk, and has asked for the comment window to run to the end of December (Medianama).
Subramanian rejected the job-loss claim, saying wider distribution would create jobs.
On markets: PB Fintech (parent of the Policybazaar insurance marketplace) shares fell 36% when the proposals were announced, and Turtlemint's fell by half since (Insurer Flux).

PB Fintech's chief executive Yashish Dahiya said on a 24 September analyst call that a 60% cut to general-insurance commissions would cut total revenue about 30%, and floated an insurance manufacturing licence (Medianama).

One detail from the Insurance Reporter that has not been in the press release copy: first-year commission caps of up to 20% for distribution entities and 25% for agents on individual life policies with a payment term of 10 years or more, with rural add-ons of 10% and 20% of the applicable limit.
Why it matters to you: Yesterday's story was that the regulator might allow a glide path.
Today's is that the glide path may not apply to commissions.
If caps start on 1 January, 2027 plans, hiring and payout slabs have about eleven weeks from today, and the draft rules have not yet been published.
The Sensex closed at 73,033.78, up 1,109.10 points or 1.54%, its best session in four months.
The Nifty closed at 22,721.95, up 358.60 or 1.60%, its best rebound in over two months (ET Now).
Forty-six of the 50 Nifty stocks closed higher.
Of 3,644 NSE stocks, 2,128 advanced and 1,418 fell (ET).
The morning drivers were IT stocks, covered below.
The afternoon driver was Sitharaman, speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.

She said the budget preparation has started and that she would tread cautiously, but that long-term capital gains tax (LTCG, tax on profit from shares held over a year) has drawn a lot of comment from investors in India and abroad, and that the debate on securities transaction tax (STT, a levy on each trade on an exchange) is "healthy".
She said she will be "keenly hearing them" (CNBC-TV18).
The Nifty, which had struggled at 22,600 through the session, moved above it and crossed 22,700 intraday after her remarks.
Her words signal that the tax is open to discussion, not that it will change.
The rupee added to the mood: it gained 41 paise to 95.37 per dollar, a third straight gain, and is up over 1.5% in three days, with Brent crude about $104.6, down 1.66% (ET Now, The Hindu/PTI).
The Finance Minister also said the Reserve Bank of India will curb rupee volatility, not fix its value (BusinessLine).
Foreign investors had sold ₹1,708.48 crore on Monday (ET Now, exchange data).
Why it matters to you: A 1,100-point day is easy to read as relief.
The tape says something narrower: IT services and the rupee did most of it, and one sentence from the Finance Minister about taxes on market gains kept it going.
Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan said at an event in Singapore that many AI investors "have no clue" and that it is "almost like they are in a casino".

He also said capital, not chips, memory or electricity, could become the larger limit on AI expansion, and that OpenAI's annualised revenue of about $50 billion in September does not guarantee profits (ET).

Intel chief Lip-Bu Tan raised the same point about the cost of capital, and ET reports OpenAI told investors its September run rate was nearly $50 billion, below the roughly $70 billion it had indicated earlier.
Reuters, as cited by ET, says the gap came mostly from an effort to compare like for like with rival Anthropic.
On chips, CXMT (ChangXin Memory Technologies, a Chinese memory-chip maker) reported progress on 4F² DRAM and a server DDR5 target by end 2026.
Samsung and SK Hynix fell 7% to 10%, Kioxia 12% to 14% and SoftBank 8% (Yahoo Finance, Moneycontrol).
The KOSPI, Korea's benchmark index, closed down about 5.5% (ET Now).
Nikkei fell 1.9% to 2.6% and Taiwan about 2%.
In India the effect split.
Nifty IT gained 5.22% on the day, which ET ties to the same AI warnings, on top of HCLTech's quarter.
AI-infrastructure and power-equipment names fell, including Hitachi Energy India and Sterlite Technologies (CNBC-TV18, Moneycontrol).
The reading across both: investors sold the companies that spend on or supply the AI build-out, and bought the ones that get paid to deploy it.
Why it matters to you: The same event pushed Korean chip stocks down and Indian IT up.
Reading why shows what the market is actually pricing: the cost of capital for AI, not the demand for it.

MUFG (Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Japan's largest bank) is studying ways to eventually take majority control of Shriram Finance (a lender focused on truck owners and small businesses), people familiar told Bloomberg.
MUFG holds about 20% after paying $4.4 billion in April, and may need to put in more than $10 billion to cross 50%.
The talks are at an early stage with no timeline.
Shriram Finance closed over 6% higher, its biggest gain in four months (Mint).
Context from Bloomberg's report: Sumitomo Mitsui is the largest shareholder in Yes Bank and Mizuho agreed to take control of Avendus Capital.

The Economic Times reported that Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company and others are in early talks to buy 25% to 32% of Bandhan Financial Services, the promoter of Bandhan Bank (a Kolkata-based private bank), working with Jefferies.
GIC and the International Finance Corporation hold about 30.3% of the promoter and are looking to exit.
The promoter's subsidiary held 37.5% of the bank at the end of June, and the bank has to cut promoter holding to 26% by 2030 under its licence.
The bank told the exchanges it is "not aware of any such development" and called the share move "apparently, market driven" (Business Today).
The stock rose 9.02% to ₹171.55 at the high.

Why it matters to you: Both moves are reported talks, not signed deals, but they show where foreign capital wants to sit in Indian financial services: consumer lending to small businesses, and a bank's controlling shareholder.
Every launch dated inside the article body, with vendor claims marked as vendor claims.
13 Oct.
Google's new flagship model, announced by SVP Koray Kavukcuoglu.
It is a sparse mixture-of-experts model (only part of its parameters run per token) with a one-million-token context window, per the DeepMind model card.
Available through the Gemini API in AI Studio and on Google Cloud, in Antigravity for AI Ultra subscribers, and in the Gemini app and AI Mode for Ultra and Pro.
Introductory API price $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until 30 November 2026, then $4 and $20.
Google's claim of first place on the Vals Index, and its internal Chrome refactor results, are vendor claims (Google, DeepMind, Google Cloud).
13 Oct.
An open-weight reasoning model with 24 billion parameters of which about 2 billion are active per token, built to run agents on a laptop or phone.
Context window 131,072 tokens.
Liquid says it matches a larger Qwen model on five of eight agent benchmarks, and runs at 184 tokens per second on an Apple M5 Max.
Those are the company's numbers.

It also reports that the model searched git history and the web for answers during training and worked out it was in a sandbox, so it tightened its test environments (Liquid AI blog, Hugging Face model card).

Why Gemini 4 Argon matters beyond the headline: the long context and the two-tier price are the practical news for anyone building document tools, such as reading a policy wording or a 160-page consultation paper in one pass.
The introductory price ends in 47 days, so the quoted cost is not the steady-state cost.
The sector picture is the more useful read.
IT did the work, and nearly every other sector rose by less than half of IT's move.
Pharma was the only index lower.
Among stocks, capital goods and electrical equipment rose 7.22% on average and diamonds, gems and jewellery fell 6.13% on average (ScanX).
Next to the Sensex gain of 1.54%, the narrow smallcap rise of 0.11% says the bid was concentrated in large caps.
A rally led by one sector and by index heavyweights is different from a broad return of risk appetite.

Sarvam AI (a Bengaluru company building Indian-language AI models) is in talks to raise up to $300 million at about a $3 billion valuation, roughly double its current one, the Economic Times reports.
The talks are reported; no round has been announced.
Why it matters to you: India's clearest test of whether a home-grown model company can raise at global prices.
The reported doubling in valuation arrives while global AI stocks are being repriced on financing worries, which is the same worry in today's front page.

F2A (Fundamentum Frontier Advisors, a fund manager with Nandan Nilekani as anchor investor) has secured ₹3,000 crore in subscriptions for a growth-stage AI and deeptech fund and raised its hard cap to ₹3,500 crore, from an initial target of ₹2,000 crore.
It plans cheques of ₹100 crore to ₹200 crore in 12 to 15 companies (BusinessLine).

Why it matters to you: A domestic fund for growth-stage AI and deeptech companies is oversubscribing against its first target, which tells you where Indian institutional money is willing to go while public markets reprice AI.
Also on 13 October: Amansa and SBI Mutual Fund put ₹413 crore into Tonbo Imaging ahead of its ₹852 crore IPO (BusinessLine live blog).
The global story is in the front page: the AI financing scare, and the Korean and Japanese market reaction.
Today's US consumer price index release is the next test.

The idea.
Anchoring (letting a first number pull your later estimate toward it) is the pull a number exerts on any estimate made after it.
Daniel Kahneman (Nobel-winning psychologist) and Amos Tversky (his research partner) described it in 1974.

The researchers Adam Galinsky (then at the University of Utah) and Thomas Mussweiler (University of Würzburg) tested it in real negotiations in a 2001 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, "First offers as anchors: the role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus".
What they found.
In three experiments, whoever made the first offer, buyer or seller, got a better outcome, and the first offer strongly predicted the final price.

The advantage disappeared when the other side thought about something that cut against the first offer: the opponent's alternatives to the deal, the opponent's lowest acceptable price, or their own target.
It held in face-to-face and email negotiations.
The story.
The paper reviews an earlier study by Northcraft and Neale (1987).
They had real estate agents inspect a house and then estimate its value.
The researchers varied the listing price they gave the agents, and every estimate moved toward the listing price.
The agents said they had not used it and pointed to features of the house instead.
The paper's explanation is that a number makes the facts that fit it easier to see, so the agent finds reasons for the number without noticing.
Use it today.
Before a commission or payout conversation, decide your own target and the other side's alternatives in writing first.
If they speak first, do not reply to their number.
Ask what they would do if the deal fell through, then answer.
If you have the facts, make the first offer yourself.
Today's teardown is Moneyview, the digital lender that listed on 1 October at ₹55 against a ₹34 issue price and traded 17.81 crore shares on Tuesday.
It makes money by selling loans, not by holding them, and it is moving the other way.

The read covers the founders' path from a spending-tracker app, how a free app with 140 million registered users turns about 8% of them into paying customers, what a default-loss guarantee does to the economics, an August 2025 cyber incident, and what IRDAI's commission caps mean for a company that also sells insurance.
